subject: 😲 Just when we thought he was out

96 
Plus: The AI bank is back | Tuesday, November 24, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Nov 24, 2026
 
 
 🤨 Everything must change so that everything can stay the same. That's one way of looking at yesterday's Nvidia bombshell and the market's reaction. Is the AI trade now back to where it was? 

 The coming days — and what happens when newly reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang goes to Capitol Hill next week — will go a long way toward answering that question. 📈📉 This morning, U.S. stock futures are down after yesterday's big Huang return rally. Asian markets were up sharply overnight.

 🗓️ Today, Emily looks at how President Trump is reshaping the market yet again, while Matt offers up a stunning stat and tallies up the winners now that Huang is back as the godfather of the AI family. 

 We have an offer you can't refuse: in 1,172 words, a 4.5-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: It's still Trump's stock market
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios The "Trump put" — the idea that you can bet on the president to make moves that will support the stock market — is back.

 Why it matters: The shock reinstatement of Nvidia's Huang , at Trump's explicit urging, is just the latest in a series of moves from the White House that have bolstered stocks.

 But the president's efforts to bring back Huang raise longer-term uncertainties about the role the U.S. government plays in picking market winners and losers. The big picture: Trump has gone much further than past presidents in trying to influence companies — directly involving himself in decisions traditionally left to corporate boards, like the hiring and firing of chief executives.

 Catch up quick: Trump in an interview yesterday wasn't shy about providing details on his involvement in getting Huang back. "I convinced 'em," Trump told CNBC .

 "I've been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it." Nvidia cited "input from senior levels of the United States government" in its statement announcing Huang's return. State of play: Trump later told the Wall Street Journal that "the response from the market has been very positive," which showed that "the decision was right."

 Nvidia's stock shot up more than 30%, and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq both surged. Reality check: In the longer term, there may be downsides.

 Investors have long favored the U.S. markets because they are seen as governed by the rule of law and independent from direct government interference. What they're saying: "The idea of having the government not just sort of regulate or intervene occasionally, but really kind of step in the middle including with personnel decisions of leadership, sounds much more like Beijing than Washington historically," says Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies China.

 The move to get Huang reinstated "creates a precedent for government to meddle more directly in the internal workings of these companies," he adds. "I've always said that the difference between the US and EM long term returns is the quality of institutions and the rule of law," said Arjun Divecha, longtime emerging markets investor at GMO, referring to emerging markets. "Regardless of the merits of the underlying facts, today's action undermines the US on both dimensions." What to watch: Even before the Huang situation, the AI trade was wobbling. The question now is whether that underlying story has fundamentally changed with its biggest booster back on stage. 

 "Jensen's return gives investors a reason to come back into the AI trade, but the industry still has to deliver on the growing skepticism of earnings sustainability," David Fetherstonhaugh, investment strategist at VistaShares, wrote in a note. Plus, Nvidia and Huang aren't out of the woods. Huang is scheduled to face questions from House lawmakers next month. "We suspect Jensen and Nvidia will remain in the crosshairs," analysts at Bernstein noted. The bottom line: One big question for investors following the Republican rout in the midterm elections was: Would Trump seek to intervene in markets when things were turning south?

 He did, after all, repeatedly reverse himself on decisions that sent markets tumbling, like the U-turn on the "liberation tariffs" that gave rise to the "TACO" acronym . "A key question is whether a constrained President Trump, entering the final phase of his tenure, becomes more willing to accept political or market disruption in pursuit of his objectives," ING analysts wrote in a note early this month. José Torres, head of economics at Interactive Brokers, also said at the time that the Trump put was gone "for now." Yesterday, I asked if his view had changed: "Yes," he said. "It's back." 
 
 
   
   
 
2. The "bank of AI" is back in business
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios AI players that have been supported by Huang's willingness to finance, invest and otherwise backstop the AI ecosystem soared on his return.

 Why it matters: Their surge highlights Nvidia's role as the linchpin of the AI trade that has powered the market in recent years. 

 State of play: Money-losing neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius — large purchasers of Nvidia processors in which Nvidia also happens to own significant stakes — soared 22.3% and 20.3%, respectively.

 Other companies that supply Nvidia or data centers and have financial ties to Nvidia also had huge days. Between the lines: Last week, Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer who was then serving as interim CEO, emphasized how the company's approach to such investments would be disciplined, rigorous and selective.

 Context: Nvidia potentially stepping back, or being more rigorous, about its investments is a big deal, as the types of companies it has often supported — like the neoclouds — have found it increasingly difficult to borrow money in bond markets, potentially curtailing their ability to keep building data centers (and buying Nvidia chips).

 The bottom line: But with yesterday's news, traders seemed to signal they see few external limits to Huang's willingness to serve as the "bank of AI" that can backstop some parts of the AI ecosystem.

 In other words, weaker AI companies again have a deep-pocketed booster with almost unchecked power to decide how he will use Nvidia's financial reserves — which belong to shareholders — as he sees fit. What's more, because his remarkable return was an explicit project of Trump, one could argue that Huang may be even more untouchable than he was before — at least for the next couple years. So is that a good thing? Well, it's an open question. In recent weeks, we've learned Huang's judgment really isn't perfect.

3. Charted: $2.8 trillion comeback
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios The big bounce in Nvidia's share price yesterday triggered the largest single-day gain in market value for a stock ever, at roughly $940 billion, according to Bloomberg . 

 Why it matters: All told, the blue-chip S&P 500 index, which climbed 4.7%, added roughly $2.8 trillion in market value on the day.

 It was the biggest daily advance for the blue chips since recovery from the April 2025 swings associated with the Trump administration's "Liberation Day" tariff announcements. Stunning stat: Monday's rally made Huang $34 billion, and shares are still about $60 below where they were on Oct. 21.
